dx: Thoracic herpes zoster with postherpetic neuralgia
case: A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of burning pain on the left side of her trunk for 4 months. Four months ago she had 2 days of tingling pain, followed by clusters of painful vesicles on an erythematous base in a band that wrapped from the left side of her lower back around to the level of the umbilicus. The rash crusted and healed within 3 weeks, but the pain has continued. Light contact from clothing over the area causes severe burning pain. She had chickenpox as a child. Physical examination shows faint hypopigmented scars in the same band, stopping at the midline, with allodynia over the scarred area. Strength and reflexes are normal. Diagnosis: thoracic herpes zoster with postherpetic neuralgia.

questions.stem: Before the rash appeared, the causative virus was most likely present in a latent state in which of the following cells?
options: Anterior horn motor neurons of the thoracic cord
Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons
Sympathetic chain ganglion neurons
Schwann cells of the intercostal nerve
approach: Childhood chickenpox followed decades later by a painful one-sided band rash points to varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reactivation.
A rash that follows one dermatome tells you the virus came down one sensory nerve.
The cell bodies of those sensory fibers sit in the dorsal root ganglion, so that is where VZV stayed latent.
questions.why: During chickenpox, VZV travels up sensory nerve fibers from the skin and stays latent in the cell bodies of sensory neurons in dorsal root ganglia and cranial nerve ganglia. When cell-mediated immunity wanes with age or immunosuppression, the virus reactivates in one ganglion and travels back down that nerve to its dermatome. That is why zoster is painful, one-sided, and stops at the midline. Reactivation in the trigeminal ganglion gives herpes zoster ophthalmicus, and reactivation in the geniculate ganglion gives Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy with ear vesicles).
whyNot: Anterior horn cells are motor neurons. Poliovirus targets them, causing flaccid weakness. Her strength is normal and her problem is sensory.
Correct.
Sympathetic ganglion neurons are autonomic. VZV latency is in sensory ganglia, which explains the dermatomal pain and rash.
Schwann cells are the target of Mycobacterium leprae, which causes patchy sensory loss. Herpesviruses stay latent in neurons.

questions.stem: She notices that firmly rubbing the skin just next to the painful band briefly lessens her pain. Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains this relief?
options: Activation of A-beta fibers that excite inhibitory interneurons
Activation of C fibers that release substance P onto projection neurons
Activation of A-delta fibers that excite lateral spinothalamic neurons
Inhibition of periaqueductal gray neurons that project to the medulla
approach: Rubbing activates large myelinated touch fibers (A-beta), not pain fibers.
Recall the gate control theory: touch fibers excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that quiet pain transmission.
Check the other options: anything that drives C or A-delta fibers or blocks descending inhibition would make pain worse.
questions.why: In the gate control model, large A-beta touch fibers send collaterals into the dorsal horn that excite inhibitory interneurons, which then reduce the output of pain projection neurons. That is why rubbing a sore area helps. Pain is also reduced from above: the periaqueductal gray activates the rostral ventromedial medulla, whose descending fibers trigger enkephalin release in the dorsal horn. Her ongoing pain after the rash healed is postherpetic neuralgia, a neuropathic pain from damage to the sensory neurons themselves, like phantom limb pain and thalamic pain.
whyNot: Correct.
C fibers carry slow burning pain and release substance P and glutamate. Activating them would increase her pain.
A-delta fibers carry fast sharp pain into the spinothalamic tract. Activating them would add pain, not relieve it.
The periaqueductal gray is the start of descending pain inhibition. Inhibiting it would remove a brake on pain and make pain worse.

questions.stem: Based on the location of her rash, reactivation most likely occurred in the ganglion of which of the following spinal nerves?
options: T6
T8
approach: Find the landmark in the case: the band reached the front of the trunk at the umbilicus.
Recall the dermatome landmarks: T4 nipple, T6 xiphoid, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal ligament.
A thoracic dermatome wraps around from the back to the front, so the whole band belongs to one root, T10.
questions.why: Each thoracic spinal nerve supplies a band of skin that runs from the back around to the front midline. The umbilicus sits in the T10 dermatome, so a zoster rash that reaches the umbilicus came from the T10 dorsal root ganglion. Other useful landmarks are C6 for the thumb, T4 for the nipple, L4 for the knee and medial leg, L5 for the dorsum of the foot, and S1 for the lateral foot. These same landmarks let you localize a root lesion from a band of sensory loss.
whyNot: T6 supplies the band at the level of the xiphoid process, above the umbilicus.
T8 supplies a band between the xiphoid and the umbilicus, above this rash.
Correct.
T12 supplies the band just above the inguinal ligament and pubic area, below the umbilicus.

questions.stem: During the 2 days of pain before the rash appeared, she was evaluated for an abdominal cause of her pain. Early visceral pain from which of the following organs is most likely to be felt in the same dermatome as her rash?
options: Esophagus
Heart
Central diaphragm
Appendix
approach: Her rash is in the T10 dermatome, around the umbilicus.
Referred pain is felt in the dermatome whose spinal segment receives the visceral afferents from that organ.
The appendix is a midgut organ whose visceral pain afferents enter about T10, so early appendicitis pain is felt around the umbilicus.
questions.why: Visceral pain fibers travel with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at specific segments. In the dorsal horn they converge on the same neurons that receive input from the skin of that segment, so the brain reads the pain as coming from the skin. Midgut organs, including the appendix, send pain afferents to about T10, so early appendicitis is felt around the umbilicus. Pain shifts to the right lower quadrant only when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic innervation. Zoster in its pre-rash phase can mimic this kind of visceral pain.
whyNot: Esophageal pain is referred to the retrosternal chest, through segments of about T4 to T6, well above T10.
Cardiac pain enters about T1 to T4 and is felt in the chest and the medial left arm.
The central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), so its irritation is felt in the shoulder.
Correct.

dx: Complete spinal cord transection at T4 with autonomic dysreflexia
case: A 27-year-old man with a complete spinal cord injury at T4 from a motorcycle collision 14 months ago is brought to the emergency department because of a severe pounding headache and blurred vision for 30 minutes. He uses an indwelling urinary catheter. His temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 46/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 214/118 mm Hg. His face and neck are flushed and sweaty; the skin of his legs is pale and cool. He has spastic paraplegia with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses, and no sensation below the nipples. The catheter tubing is kinked and the bladder is distended. Diagnosis: complete spinal cord transection at T4 with autonomic dysreflexia.

questions.stem: On the day of his injury, which of the following findings was most likely present in his legs?
options: Spastic tone with brisk tendon reflexes
Flaccid tone with absent tendon reflexes
Fasciculations with marked muscle atrophy
Normal tone with intact tendon reflexes
approach: Recognize that he now has upper motor neuron signs, the late phase of a cord transection.
Recall that right after transection the cord below the lesion goes silent (spinal shock).
Spinal shock gives flaccid paralysis and areflexia, which later changes to spasticity and hyperreflexia.
questions.why: Spinal shock follows acute cord transection. The cord below the lesion suddenly loses descending excitatory input, so motor neurons become unresponsive. The result is flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes, and, with injuries above about T6, neurogenic hypotension from lost sympathetic tone. Over days to weeks, reflex circuits below the lesion recover and become overactive, producing spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia and Babinski signs. A thoracic injury causes paraplegia, while injury at or above C3 also cuts the phrenic outflow (C3 to C5) and requires a ventilator.
whyNot: Spasticity with brisk reflexes is the late phase, which he has now. It develops after spinal shock fades.
Correct.
Fasciculations and marked atrophy are lower motor neuron signs. A cord transection at T4 leaves the lumbar motor neurons intact.
A complete transection removes all descending control, so tone and reflexes cannot stay normal on the day of injury.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his slow heart rate during this episode?
options: Sympathetic discharge from spinal segments below the lesion
Release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Reduced venous return from dilation of leg veins
Baroreceptor reflex raising vagal output to the heart
approach: The stimulus (a distended bladder) is below the lesion, so it triggers a spinal sympathetic reflex that cannot be damped from above.
Widespread vasoconstriction below the lesion causes severe hypertension.
The intact brainstem senses the high pressure through baroreceptors and slows the heart through the vagus nerve, which is not affected by the cord injury.
questions.why: Autonomic dysreflexia occurs with cord injuries at or above about T6, above the splanchnic sympathetic outflow. A noxious stimulus below the lesion, most often a full bladder or bowel, sets off a large spinal sympathetic reflex. Descending inhibitory signals cannot reach the cord, so vessels below the lesion clamp down and blood pressure soars. Baroreceptors signal the brainstem, which raises vagal tone (slowing the heart) and dilates vessels above the lesion (flushing and sweating of the face). The vagus leaves the brainstem directly, so the cord lesion does not block it.
whyNot: The sympathetic discharge below the lesion explains the hypertension and pale cold legs, but sympathetic input would speed the heart, not slow it.
Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla raises the heart rate through beta-1 receptors.
The leg vessels constrict during dysreflexia, and reduced venous return would lower blood pressure and raise heart rate.
Correct.

questions.stem: The rise in his blood pressure is first detected by stretch receptors in the carotid sinus. Which of the following describes the nerve that carries this signal and the nucleus where it first synapses?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve to the nucleus solitarius
Vagus nerve to the nucleus ambiguus
Glossopharyngeal nerve to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
Vagus nerve to the nucleus solitarius
approach: Separate the two baroreceptor sites: carotid sinus versus aortic arch.
Carotid sinus afferents travel in the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); aortic arch afferents travel in the vagus (CN X).
All visceral sensory input from CN VII, IX, and X ends in the nucleus solitarius.
questions.why: The carotid sinus sits at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery and is supplied by the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of CN IX. The aortic arch baroreceptors send their signals in CN X. Both nerves carry these visceral sensory fibers to the nucleus solitarius in the medulla, which then adjusts sympathetic and vagal output. Visceral pain afferents follow a different route: they travel with autonomic nerves to the spinal cord. His bladder afferents enter the cord below the T4 lesion, so the bladder distension never reaches conscious awareness.
whyNot: Correct.
The vagus does carry aortic arch signals, but the nucleus ambiguus is a motor nucleus for the pharynx, larynx, and part of the cardiac vagal output.
The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus is an efferent parasympathetic nucleus. It sends signals out, not in.
This is the route for aortic arch baroreceptors. The stem specifies the carotid sinus, which uses CN IX.

questions.stem: Another patient on the spinal injury unit has a stab wound that cut the right half of the spinal cord at T10. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Right leg weakness with loss of vibration sense in the left leg
Left leg weakness with loss of pain sense in the right leg
Right leg weakness with loss of pain sense in the left leg
Loss of pain sense in both legs with vibration sense preserved
approach: A cut through half the cord is a Brown-Sequard hemisection.
The corticospinal tract and dorsal columns cross in the medulla, so their deficits are on the same side as the lesion.
The spinothalamic tract crosses within one or two segments of entry, so pain and temperature loss is on the opposite side.
questions.why: In a hemisection, the lateral corticospinal tract and the dorsal columns are cut on the side of the lesion, and at the spinal level both tracts serve the same side of the body (they cross in the medulla). That gives weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the right. Pain and temperature fibers from the left leg have already crossed to the right spinothalamic tract, so they are cut too, giving loss of pain and temperature in the left leg starting one or two segments below the lesion. Bilateral loss of pain with preserved touch is the pattern of syringomyelia, a central cord lesion.
whyNot: Weakness is ipsilateral, but vibration loss is also ipsilateral because the dorsal columns do not cross until the medulla.
This reverses the sides. Motor loss is on the side of the lesion, and pain loss is on the opposite side.
Correct.
Bilateral pain loss with preserved vibration fits a central cord lesion such as syringomyelia, which usually gives a cape-like pattern in the arms.

case: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of an unsteady gait that is worse in the dark and brief, stabbing pains in his legs. He has fallen three times. Physical examination shows a wide-based, stamping gait. He sways and falls when he closes his eyes while standing with feet together. Vibration and position sense are absent in the feet. Patellar and ankle reflexes are absent. Strength is normal. Both pupils are small and irregular; they constrict with near focus but not to light. Serum rapid plasma reagin is reactive. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 22 lymphocytes/mm3 (normal 0 to 5) and a reactive VDRL test. Diagnosis: tabes dorsalis (tertiary neurosyphilis).

questions.stem: Degeneration of which of the following structures most directly explains his positive Romberg sign?
options: Lateral corticospinal tracts
Anterior horn motor neurons
Cerebellar vermis Purkinje cells
Dorsal roots and dorsal columns
approach: A positive Romberg sign means the patient can balance with vision but not without it, so the problem is lost proprioception.
Proprioception from the legs enters through the dorsal roots and ascends in the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis).
Tabes dorsalis destroys exactly these: the dorsal roots and the dorsal columns of the lower cord.
questions.why: In tabes dorsalis, Treponema pallidum damages the dorsal roots, and the dorsal columns that carry those fibers then degenerate. Without position sense from the legs, the patient relies on vision to stay upright, so he falls when his eyes close (positive Romberg sign). Loss of the reflex afferents in the dorsal roots explains the absent reflexes, and irritation of the roots gives lightning pains. Other tertiary findings are Argyll Robertson pupils, Charcot joints, and, in other forms, general paresis and meningovascular stroke. CSF VDRL is specific for neurosyphilis.
whyNot: Corticospinal tract damage causes weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski signs. He has normal strength and absent reflexes.
Anterior horn cell loss causes weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations. His strength is normal.
Cerebellar ataxia is present with eyes open and does not worsen much with eye closure, so the Romberg test is usually negative.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the organism that caused his disease?
options: Acid-fast bacillus with an armadillo reservoir
Spirochete detected by darkfield microscopy
Gram-positive bacillus that forms terminal spores
Encapsulated yeast seen with India ink stain
approach: Tabes dorsalis with a reactive CSF VDRL means tertiary syphilis.
The cause is Treponema pallidum, a thin spirochete.
It is too thin to see on Gram stain, so it is seen with darkfield microscopy or fluorescent antibody and confirmed by treponemal tests such as FTA-ABS.
questions.why: Treponema pallidum is a thin, tightly coiled spirochete that does not grow in routine culture and does not show on Gram stain. In a primary chancre or secondary lesion it is seen by darkfield microscopy. Infection is screened with nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR), which detect antibody to cardiolipin, and confirmed with treponemal tests such as FTA-ABS. Borrelia burgdorferi is another spirochete, spread by Ixodes ticks. Mycobacterium leprae is an acid-fast rod that prefers cool body sites and infects Schwann cells.
whyNot: This is Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy with patchy skin anesthesia and thickened nerves. Armadillos are its reservoir in the US.
Correct.
This describes Clostridium tetani, whose toxin blocks inhibitory interneurons and causes spastic paralysis, not sensory ataxia.
This is Cryptococcus neoformans, a cause of chronic meningitis in people with AIDS. It does not cause tabes dorsalis.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl has a 3-year history of progressive gait ataxia. Examination shows absent ankle reflexes, loss of vibration sense in the feet, a positive Romberg sign, extensor plantar responses, high foot arches, and scoliosis. Echocardiography shows hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Serologic testing for syphilis is nonreactive. Which of the following is the most likely genetic cause of her condition?
options: CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene
CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene
GAA repeat expansion in the frataxin gene
CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene
approach: Like tabes, she has dorsal column loss and areflexia, but she also has Babinski signs, pes cavus, scoliosis, and cardiomyopathy in adolescence.
This combination is Friedreich ataxia.
Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive and caused by a GAA trinucleotide expansion in the frataxin gene.
questions.why: Friedreich ataxia is the most common inherited ataxia. A GAA repeat expansion in an intron of the frataxin gene reduces frataxin, a mitochondrial protein needed for iron-sulfur cluster assembly. Iron builds up in mitochondria and oxidative damage kills neurons. The dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal tracts degenerate, together with dorsal root ganglion cells, so the patient has sensory ataxia, absent reflexes, and Babinski signs at the same time. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (the usual cause of death), diabetes, kyphoscoliosis, and pes cavus complete the picture.
whyNot: CAG expansion in huntingtin causes Huntington disease, with chorea and dementia in mid-adult life and autosomal dominant inheritance.
CTG expansion in DMPK causes myotonic dystrophy, with myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, and frontal balding.
Correct.
CGG expansion in FMR1 causes fragile X syndrome, with intellectual disability, a long face, and large testes.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man who has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years has 6 weeks of rapidly worsening numbness in all four limbs and an unsteady gait. Examination shows loss of vibration and position sense in the hands and feet, absent reflexes, a positive Romberg sign, and normal strength. Syphilis serology is nonreactive. CT of the chest shows a central hilar mass. Antibodies against which of the following are most likely present?
options: Hu antigen in neuronal nuclei
Yo antigen in Purkinje cells
NMDA receptors on cortical neurons
Voltage-gated calcium channels on nerve terminals
approach: A smoker with a central hilar mass most likely has small cell lung cancer.
Rapid, purely sensory loss in all limbs with sensory ataxia means the dorsal root ganglion neurons are being destroyed (sensory neuronopathy).
Small cell lung cancer expresses the neuronal Hu antigen, and the immune response against it attacks dorsal root ganglion neurons.
questions.why: Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes occur when a tumor expresses a protein normally found only in neurons. The immune response against the tumor also attacks the matching neurons, mostly through cytotoxic T cells, with the antibody serving as a marker. Small cell lung cancer expresses Hu proteins, and anti-Hu disease destroys dorsal root ganglion neurons (sensory neuronopathy) and can cause limbic encephalitis. Anti-Yo antibodies, usually from ovarian or breast cancer, cause cerebellar degeneration. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is linked to ovarian teratoma.
whyNot: Correct.
Anti-Yo antibodies cause subacute cerebellar degeneration, usually with ovarian or breast cancer. That gives cerebellar ataxia, not loss of position sense.
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis causes psychiatric symptoms, seizures, and dyskinesias, typically in young women with ovarian teratoma.
Antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome, also linked to small cell lung cancer, but it causes proximal weakness, not sensory loss.

case: A 64-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her husband because of rapidly worsening memory and confusion over 3 months. She now needs help dressing and walks unsteadily. She has no family history of neurologic disease, and she has had no surgery or transfusions. Her temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F). She is disoriented and cannot recall any of three words. Sudden noises cause brief myoclonic jerks of her arms. Gait is ataxic. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 2 cells/mm3 (normal 0 to 5), normal glucose and protein, and an elevated 14-3-3 protein. Diffusion-weighted MRI shows ribbon-like cortical and caudate hyperintensity. EEG shows periodic sharp wave complexes. Diagnosis: sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following molecular changes most likely underlies her disease?
options: Refolding of alpha-helical PrP into beta-pleated PrP
Hyperphosphorylation of tau into neurofibrillary tangles
Deposition of amyloid-beta in neuritic plaques
Polyglutamine expansion within huntingtin protein
approach: Rapid dementia over months with myoclonus, elevated CSF 14-3-3, and periodic sharp waves on EEG points to prion disease.
Prion disease is caused by misfolded prion protein, not a virus or bacterium.
The misfolded protein turns normal alpha-helical PrP into beta-pleated PrP, which resists proteases and builds up.
questions.why: Normal prion protein (PrPc) is a membrane protein rich in alpha helices. In prion disease, it changes into a beta-pleated form (PrPsc) that resists protease digestion and acts as a template that converts more normal PrP. The protein accumulates and kills neurons, leaving spongiform vacuoles in gray matter without inflammation. Most cases are sporadic, some are inherited (PRNP mutations), and some are acquired, such as variant CJD from eating beef contaminated with bovine prions and iatrogenic CJD from contaminated neurosurgical instruments or dura mater grafts.
whyNot: Correct.
Tau tangles are part of Alzheimer disease, which progresses over years, without early myoclonus or periodic sharp waves.
Amyloid-beta plaques are the other hallmark of Alzheimer disease, a slowly progressive dementia.
Polyglutamine expansion in huntingtin causes Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant disorder with chorea. She has no family history.

questions.stem: For comparison, the laboratory records an EEG from a healthy 40-year-old volunteer who is lying awake and relaxed with her eyes closed. She is then asked to open her eyes and solve arithmetic problems. Which of the following changes over the occipital region is most likely?
options: Alpha rhythm replaced by high-amplitude delta waves
Theta rhythm replaced by alpha waves
Alpha rhythm replaced by low-voltage beta activity
Beta activity replaced by alpha waves
approach: Identify the starting state: awake and relaxed with eyes closed gives a posterior alpha rhythm (8 to 13 Hz).
Identify the new state: eyes open and mentally alert gives low-voltage, fast beta activity (above 13 Hz).
So the alpha rhythm disappears and beta takes over (alpha blocking). Theta and delta belong to sleep, not to an alert adult.
questions.why: The EEG frequency follows the level of arousal. Closing the eyes and relaxing brings out an alpha rhythm (8 to 13 Hz) over the occipital lobes. Opening the eyes or concentrating blocks the alpha rhythm and replaces it with low-voltage, fast beta activity. Drowsiness and stage N1 sleep show theta waves, N2 shows sleep spindles and K complexes, and N3 (deep sleep) shows high-amplitude delta waves. REM sleep returns to low-voltage, beta-like activity. The slow, disorganized background in an awake patient like her points to a widespread cortical disorder, such as prion disease.
whyNot: High-amplitude delta waves mark deep N3 sleep. Opening the eyes and doing mental work makes the EEG faster, not slower.
Theta waves appear with drowsiness and N1 sleep. A relaxed adult with eyes closed shows alpha, and alerting her makes the EEG faster than alpha.
Correct.
This is the reverse change, seen when an alert person closes the eyes and relaxes.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has had 8 months of declining school performance, personality change, and repetitive jerks of his arms. He had measles at 14 months of age, before any vaccination. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid findings is most likely in this patient?
options: JC virus DNA detected by PCR
High titer of antibody to measles virus
Albuminocytologic dissociation
Neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose
approach: Progressive cognitive decline and myoclonus in a child years after early measles infection points to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE).
SSPE is a persistent infection with a defective measles virus that cannot bud from neurons.
The immune system keeps responding, so CSF shows very high anti-measles antibody levels.
questions.why: In SSPE, measles virus acquired early in life persists in the brain years later as a defective virus, often with mutations in the matrix (M) protein, so it spreads from cell to cell without forming new virus particles. The ongoing infection causes inflammation, demyelination, and neuron loss with inclusion bodies. Children develop behavior change, cognitive decline, and myoclonus, then progress to death. The diagnosis rests on high anti-measles antibody titers in CSF, often with periodic complexes on EEG. Measles infection before age 2 is a major risk factor.
whyNot: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in severely immunosuppressed patients, not in a healthy child after measles.
Correct.
High protein with a normal cell count is the CSF pattern of Guillain-Barre syndrome, which causes ascending weakness.
Neutrophils with low glucose indicate acute bacterial meningitis, which develops over hours to days with fever and neck stiffness.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has 18 months of cognitive decline with marked day-to-day swings in alertness. He describes seeing small children playing in his living room. Examination shows mild rigidity and slow finger tapping. He dies 5 years later. Which of the following findings is most likely on examination of his cerebral cortex at autopsy?
options: Spongiform vacuoles in gray matter without inflammation
Round tau-positive inclusions in frontal neurons
Tau aggregates in midbrain and basal ganglia neurons
Alpha-synuclein inclusions in cortical neurons
approach: Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism define dementia with Lewy bodies.
The slower course over years separates it from prion disease.
Lewy bodies are alpha-synuclein inclusions; in this disorder they are found in cortical neurons.
questions.why: Dementia with Lewy bodies is a synucleinopathy, like Parkinson disease, but the alpha-synuclein inclusions are widespread in the cortex as well as the brainstem. Its core features are fluctuating attention, recurrent detailed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder. Dementia appears before or within about a year of parkinsonism. Frontotemporal dementia starts with personality or language change and shows tau (Pick bodies) or TDP-43 inclusions. Progressive supranuclear palsy is a tauopathy with vertical gaze palsy and early falls.
whyNot: Spongiform change without inflammation is prion disease, which progresses over months, not years, and lacks prominent hallucinations.
Round tau inclusions (Pick bodies) mark frontotemporal dementia, which begins with personality change or language loss.
Tau in the midbrain and basal ganglia fits progressive supranuclear palsy, with vertical gaze palsy and early falls.
Correct.

case: A 43-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because he woke up this morning with drooping of the right side of his face. Yesterday he had aching pain behind his right ear. He reports that sounds seem too loud in his right ear and that food tastes strange. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows that he cannot wrinkle his right forehead, close his right eye fully, or raise the right corner of his mouth. The right nasolabial fold is flat. There are no vesicles in the ear canal or on the palate. The rest of the neurologic examination is normal. Diagnosis: Bell palsy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most commonly proposed cause of this patient's condition?
options: Antibodies against GM1 ganglioside
Compression by a cerebellopontine angle tumor
Nerve swelling after HSV-1 reactivation
Invasion by a parotid gland carcinoma
approach: Sudden whole-face weakness on one side with hyperacusis and taste change, developing overnight, fits Bell palsy.
Bell palsy is idiopathic, but the leading explanation is reactivation of herpes simplex virus in the geniculate ganglion.
The inflamed nerve swells inside the narrow facial canal, which compresses it.
questions.why: Bell palsy is an acute lower motor neuron palsy of CN VII without another identified cause. Reactivation of latent HSV-1 in the geniculate ganglion is the most widely accepted trigger. The nerve becomes inflamed and swollen inside the bony facial canal, where it has little room. It is more common with diabetes and pregnancy, and Lyme disease must be excluded in endemic areas. Because the lesion is in the canal, branches to the stapedius (hyperacusis), chorda tympani (anterior tongue taste), and lacrimal gland (tearing) can be affected along with all facial muscles.
whyNot: Anti-GM1 antibodies are linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome, which can cause facial weakness but usually bilateral and with ascending limb weakness.
A tumor at the cerebellopontine angle, such as a vestibular schwannoma, causes slowly progressive hearing loss and tinnitus, not overnight facial palsy.
Correct.
Parotid carcinoma can invade the facial nerve, but weakness develops gradually and there would be a parotid mass. It also spares taste and hearing.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient best distinguishes his lesion from an infarct in the left primary motor cortex?
options: Drooping of the right corner of the mouth
Flattening of the right nasolabial fold
Weak puffing of the right cheek
Weakness of the right frontalis muscle
approach: A cortical lesion is an upper motor neuron lesion; Bell palsy is a lower motor neuron lesion of CN VII.
The part of the facial nucleus that controls the upper face receives input from both hemispheres; the part for the lower face gets input mainly from the opposite cortex.
So a cortical stroke spares the forehead, while a CN VII lesion weakens the forehead too.
questions.why: Corticobulbar fibers to the facial motor neurons for the forehead come from both motor cortices, so one cortex can still move the forehead if the other is damaged. Neurons for the lower face receive mostly crossed input. A stroke in the left motor cortex therefore weakens only the right lower face and spares the forehead. A lesion of the facial nucleus or the nerve itself cuts the final common pathway to every muscle on that side, so the forehead is weak as well. This is the quickest bedside test to separate a central from a peripheral facial palsy.
whyNot: Mouth droop is caused by lower face weakness, which occurs in both a cortical stroke and a facial nerve lesion.
A flat nasolabial fold is also a lower face sign and occurs with both lesions.
Buccinator weakness affects the lower face and is present with both upper and lower motor neuron lesions.
Correct.

topics: Upper versus lower motor neuron facial palsy

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman who lives in Connecticut has weakness of both sides of her face and headache for 4 days. Five weeks ago, after a hiking trip, she had an expanding red rash with central clearing on her thigh. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 110 cells/mm3 (normal 0 to 5), mostly lymphocytes. Her illness was most likely acquired by which of the following routes?
options: Bite of an Ixodes tick
Exposure to water contaminated by rat urine
Sexual contact with an infected partner
Bite of an Aedes mosquito
approach: Bilateral facial palsy with lymphocytic meningitis after an expanding ring-shaped rash is early disseminated Lyme disease.
Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi.
It is spread by Ixodes (deer) ticks, common in the northeastern US.
questions.why: Lyme neuroborreliosis develops weeks after the tick bite and the erythema migrans rash. Its classic triad is facial nerve palsy (often bilateral), lymphocytic meningitis, and painful radiculopathy. Bilateral facial palsy is unusual for Bell palsy and should raise suspicion of Lyme disease. Borrelia burgdorferi is carried by Ixodes ticks, which acquire it from white-footed mice, while deer host the adult ticks. Leptospirosis, the other spirochetal cause of meningitis, comes from water contaminated by animal urine.
whyNot: Correct.
Water contaminated by rodent or animal urine spreads Leptospira, which causes fever, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, and sometimes meningitis, but not erythema migrans.
Sexual contact spreads Treponema pallidum. Syphilis can cause meningitis and cranial neuropathies, but the rash is not an expanding ring.
Aedes mosquitoes spread dengue, Zika, and chikungunya viruses, which do not cause erythema migrans.

questions.stem: Three days after his visit, the man with Bell palsy reports pain, a gritty feeling, and watering in his right eye. Which of the following findings is most likely on examination of the right eye?
options: Blood layering in the anterior chamber
Corneal defect that stains with fluorescein
Painless bright red patch under the conjunctiva
Restricted upward gaze with double vision
approach: He cannot close the right eye fully, and Bell palsy can reduce tear production.
An eye that stays partly open and dry loses its protective tear film, so the corneal epithelium breaks down (exposure keratopathy).
A corneal epithelial defect causes pain and foreign body sensation and takes up fluorescein dye.
questions.why: The orbicularis oculi closes the eye and spreads tears over the cornea with each blink. With CN VII weakness, the eye stays partly open, and the lacrimal gland may lose its parasympathetic drive through the greater petrosal nerve. The corneal epithelium dries and erodes, producing pain, a gritty sensation, reflex tearing, and redness. Fluorescein dye pools where the epithelium is missing and glows green under cobalt blue light. Corneal abrasion from a scratch or foreign body looks the same on staining.
whyNot: Blood in the anterior chamber (hyphema) follows blunt eye trauma, which he did not have.
Correct.
Subconjunctival hemorrhage is a painless red patch from a ruptured conjunctival vessel, often after coughing or straining. It does not cause a gritty feeling.
Limited upward gaze with diplopia follows an orbital floor fracture that traps the inferior rectus after blunt facial trauma.

case: A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of numbness and tingling in her right thumb, index finger, and middle finger for 6 weeks. The symptoms wake her at night and improve when she shakes her hand. She has mild swelling of both hands and ankles. Her blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows decreased sensation over the palmar surfaces of the right thumb, index finger, middle finger, and the lateral half of the ring finger. Sensation over the thenar eminence is normal. Thumb abduction is mildly weak. Tapping over the volar wrist and holding the wrists fully flexed for 60 seconds both reproduce the tingling. Diagnosis: carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient best localizes the nerve compression to the wrist rather than to the forearm?
options: Weak flexion at the thumb interphalangeal joint
Normal sensation over the thenar eminence
Weak pronation of the forearm
Numbness over the medial palm and little finger
approach: Her symptoms follow the median nerve distribution, made worse at night and by wrist flexion.
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves the nerve above the wrist and passes over the flexor retinaculum, not through the carpal tunnel.
So spared sensation over the thenar eminence means the compression is inside the tunnel.
questions.why: In carpal tunnel syndrome, the median nerve is squeezed under the flexor retinaculum along with nine flexor tendons. Anything that raises pressure in the tunnel can cause it: fluid retention in pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid synovitis, diabetes, and dialysis-related amyloid. Symptoms are paresthesia of the thumb to the lateral ring finger, worse at night, with Tinel and Phalen signs and later thenar atrophy. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel, so sensation over the thenar palm is spared. A more proximal median nerve lesion would numb the palm too.
whyNot: Flexor pollicis longus is supplied in the forearm by the anterior interosseous branch, so its weakness points to a lesion above the wrist.
Correct.
Pronator teres and pronator quadratus are supplied in the forearm, so pronation stays normal in carpal tunnel syndrome.
The medial palm and little finger are supplied by the ulnar nerve, which runs outside the carpal tunnel.

questions.stem: The compressed nerve in this patient is formed from which of the following parts of the brachial plexus?
options: Lateral and medial cords
Lateral and posterior cords
Medial and posterior cords
Posterior cord only
approach: Identify the nerve: median nerve, from the sensory pattern and thenar weakness.
Recall the terminal branches: lateral cord gives musculocutaneous, medial cord gives ulnar, posterior cord gives axillary and radial.
The median nerve is formed by one root from the lateral cord and one from the medial cord, carrying C6 to T1 fibers (with some C5).
questions.why: The brachial plexus runs from roots (C5 to T1) to trunks, divisions, cords, and branches. The median nerve forms from a lateral root from the lateral cord and a medial root from the medial cord, which join in front of the axillary artery. The posterior cord gives the axillary and radial nerves. Upper trunk injury (Erb palsy, C5 to C6) causes the waiter's tip posture. Lower trunk injury (Klumpke palsy, C8 to T1) weakens the intrinsic hand muscles and can cause a claw hand.
whyNot: Correct.
The posterior cord does not contribute to the median nerve. It forms the radial and axillary nerves.
The median nerve does get a medial cord root, but nothing from the posterior cord.
The posterior cord alone gives rise to the radial and axillary nerves, which supply the extensors and deltoid.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman who is a competitive swimmer has 5 months of tingling along the right medial forearm and little finger, right hand weakness, and coolness and fatigue of the right arm when she raises it overhead. Examination shows mild wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles. X-ray of the cervical spine shows a cervical rib on the right. Compression of which of the following structures most likely explains her neurologic findings?
options: Median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum
Ulnar nerve within the cubital tunnel
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
Lower trunk of the brachial plexus
approach: A cervical rib, overhead arm symptoms, and vascular signs point to thoracic outlet syndrome.
The lowest part of the brachial plexus lies on the first rib or cervical rib and is the part most often compressed.
Lower trunk fibers (C8 to T1) supply the medial forearm skin and the intrinsic hand muscles.
questions.why: In thoracic outlet syndrome, the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8 to T1), the subclavian artery, or the subclavian vein is compressed as it passes over the first rib, usually by a cervical rib or tight scalene muscles. Lower trunk compression causes paresthesia along the ulnar side of the forearm and hand and weakness and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles. Arterial compression causes coolness, pallor, and fatigue with arm elevation. The medial forearm sensory loss helps separate it from an ulnar nerve lesion.
whyNot: The median nerve at the wrist causes symptoms in the thumb to the ring finger and spares the medial forearm.
Ulnar compression at the elbow numbs the little finger and weakens the hand intrinsics, but it spares the medial forearm and does not cause vascular symptoms.
Upper trunk (C5 to C6) compression weakens shoulder abduction and elbow flexion and causes lateral arm numbness.
Correct.

questions.stem: She reports that she can no longer feel a light object slipping across her right fingertips. Which of the following best describes the receptor most responsible for detecting this stimulus?
options: Slowly adapting disc at the base of the epidermis
Rapidly adapting corpuscle deep in the dermis and subcutis
Rapidly adapting corpuscle in the dermal papillae
Slowly adapting spindle-shaped ending that senses skin stretch
approach: A light moving touch on glabrous skin is a change in stimulus, so it needs a rapidly adapting receptor near the surface.
Meissner corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae of fingertips, adapt rapidly, and respond to light touch, flutter, and slip.
All four skin mechanoreceptors send signals through large myelinated A-beta fibers, so fiber type does not separate them.
questions.why: Skin mechanoreceptors differ by depth and adaptation. Meissner corpuscles are superficial in the dermal papillae of hairless skin, adapt rapidly, and detect light stroking, low-frequency vibration, and an object slipping in the grip. Merkel discs are superficial but slowly adapting and signal sustained pressure, edges, and texture. Pacinian corpuscles lie deep, adapt very rapidly, and sense high-frequency vibration. Ruffini endings are deep, slowly adapting, and sense skin stretch. Free nerve endings carry pain and temperature on A-delta and C fibers.
whyNot: This is the Merkel disc, which signals steady pressure and fine form, not a moving stimulus.
This is the Pacinian corpuscle, which senses high-frequency vibration and deep pressure.
Correct.
This is the Ruffini ending, which senses sustained stretch of the skin and joint position.

dx: L5-S1 disc herniation with S1 radiculopathy and sciatica
case: A 44-year-old man who works in a warehouse comes to the physician because of low back pain that radiates down the back of his left thigh and calf to the outer edge of his foot. The pain began 5 days ago while he was lifting a heavy box and worsens with coughing. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows that raising his straightened left leg to 40 degrees reproduces pain shooting below the knee. Sensation is decreased over the lateral left foot and sole. Plantar flexion of the left foot is weak, and the left ankle reflex is absent. Perianal sensation and bladder function are normal. MRI shows a posterolateral herniation of the L5-S1 disc compressing the left S1 nerve root. Diagnosis: L5-S1 disc herniation with S1 radiculopathy and sciatica.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this posterolateral L5-S1 herniation compresses the S1 nerve root rather than the L5 nerve root?
options: The ligamentum flavum shields the L5 root
The S1 root exits the canal above the L5-S1 disc
The posterior longitudinal ligament is widest laterally
The L5 root exits the canal above the L5-S1 disc
approach: A herniated disc is nucleus pulposus pushing through a tear in the annulus fibrosus.
The posterior longitudinal ligament is strong in the midline, so most herniations go posterolateral.
Each lumbar root exits under the pedicle of its own vertebra, above the disc, so a posterolateral disc hits the next lower root as it passes by.
questions.why: Lumbar nerve roots run down inside the canal and leave through the foramen below the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra. The L5 root leaves through the L5-S1 foramen in its upper part, above the disc. The S1 root is still passing down in the lateral recess at the L5-S1 disc level, so a posterolateral L5-S1 herniation compresses S1. In the same way, an L4-L5 herniation affects L5. Most herniations occur at L4-L5 or L5-S1, where the spine bears the most load and motion.
whyNot: The ligamentum flavum lines the back of the canal. It does not protect the L5 root; thickening of it can actually narrow the canal.
The S1 root exits through the first sacral foramen, below the L5-S1 disc. That is why it is still in the path of this herniation.
The posterior longitudinal ligament is strongest in the midline and narrow at the sides, which is why discs herniate posterolaterally. It does not decide which root is compressed.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why raising his straightened left leg reproduces his pain?
options: It raises pressure in the lumbar cerebrospinal fluid
It stretches the compressed root over the disc
It contracts the piriformis around the sciatic nerve
It compresses the facet joints of the lower lumbar spine
approach: Pain from the buttock down the back of the thigh to below the knee is sciatica, usually from L5 or S1 root compression.
Hip flexion with a straight knee pulls the sciatic nerve and its L4 to S1 roots downward.
A root tethered over a herniated disc cannot slide, so stretching it reproduces radiating pain, usually between about 30 and 70 degrees.
questions.why: Sciatica is radiating pain along the course of the sciatic nerve, from the buttock down the back of the thigh and below the knee. It usually comes from compression of the L5 or S1 root by a herniated disc. In the straight leg raise test, flexing the hip with the knee straight stretches the sciatic nerve and pulls its roots through the foramina. If a root is already stretched over a disc, the extra tension produces pain that shoots below the knee. Pain felt only in the back or hamstrings does not count as a positive test.
whyNot: Coughing and straining raise CSF and epidural pressure, which is why his pain worsens with coughing, but the straight leg raise works by stretching the root.
Correct.
Piriformis tightness can irritate the sciatic nerve in the buttock, but it would not explain the MRI finding or the absent ankle reflex.
Facet joint pain is local back pain that worsens with spinal extension. The straight leg raise does not load the facets.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman develops weakness lifting her right foot after sitting with her legs crossed for a long flight. She trips over her toes when she walks. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor a common fibular nerve injury over an L5 radiculopathy?
options: Normal strength of foot inversion
Weak ankle dorsiflexion
Numbness of the dorsum of the foot
Weak extension of the great toe
approach: Foot drop can come from the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck or from the L5 root.
Both lesions weaken the dorsiflexors and toe extensors and numb the dorsum of the foot, so those findings do not separate them.
Foot inversion uses tibialis posterior, supplied by the tibial nerve but still from L5. It is weak in L5 radiculopathy and normal in fibular nerve injury.
questions.why: The common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck, where leg crossing, casts, or fractures can compress it. It supplies the dorsiflexors and toe extensors (deep fibular) and the evertors (superficial fibular), and the skin of the dorsum of the foot. L5 supplies these same muscles but also tibialis posterior (inversion, through the tibial nerve) and gluteus medius (hip abduction, through the superior gluteal nerve). So weak inversion or hip abduction points to the root. Superior gluteal nerve injury alone gives a Trendelenburg sign.
whyNot: Correct.
Dorsiflexion weakness causes foot drop in both lesions, so it cannot tell them apart.
Dorsal foot numbness occurs with both, because the fibular nerve carries L5 fibers to that skin.
Extensor hallucis longus is weak in both lesions. It is a sensitive test for L5 but not specific for the root.

questions.stem: Two days later, he returns because he cannot urinate and has numbness of his buttocks and perineum. MRI shows a large central extrusion of the L5-S1 disc filling the spinal canal. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?
options: Extensor plantar responses in both feet
Sensory level at the umbilicus
Absent anal wink reflex
Brisk patellar reflexes in both legs
approach: Urinary retention with saddle anesthesia after a central disc extrusion means cauda equina syndrome.
The spinal cord ends at about L1 to L2, so at L5-S1 only nerve roots are compressed.
Root compression gives lower motor neuron signs: reduced or absent reflexes, including the anal wink reflex (S2 to S4).
questions.why: Below the conus medullaris, the canal contains only the lumbosacral roots of the cauda equina. A large central disc, tumor, or epidural abscess at this level compresses several roots on both sides. The result is saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, loss of anal sphincter tone and the anal wink reflex, and lower motor neuron weakness with reduced reflexes in the legs. Spinal cord compression higher up gives the opposite: a sensory level, upper motor neuron signs such as spasticity, brisk reflexes, and Babinski signs. Both are surgical emergencies.
whyNot: Babinski signs are upper motor neuron signs. They come from cord compression above the conus, not root compression at L5-S1.
A sensory level at the umbilicus means the cord is compressed near T10, well above this lesion.
Correct.
Brisk reflexes are an upper motor neuron sign. Cauda equina compression reduces reflexes.

case: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the onset of severe pain in her left eye, which began while she was watching a film in a dark theater. She has blurred vision in that eye, sees colored halos around lights, and has vomited twice. She has worn glasses for farsightedness since childhood. Her temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 156/88 mm Hg. The left eye shows conjunctival redness around the cornea, a hazy cornea, a shallow anterior chamber, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. Intraocular pressure is 58 mm Hg in the left eye (normal 10 to 21) and 17 mm Hg in the right. Diagnosis: acute angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following most directly caused the rise in her intraocular pressure?
options: Iris pressed against the trabecular meshwork
Increased aqueous secretion by the ciliary body
Slowly rising resistance within the meshwork
Blood cells obstructing the trabecular meshwork
approach: In the dark the pupil dilates, and in a mid-dilated position the iris presses on the lens, blocking aqueous flow through the pupil (pupillary block).
Pressure builds behind the iris and pushes the peripheral iris forward against the trabecular meshwork.
With the angle closed, aqueous cannot drain and pressure rises within hours.
questions.why: Aqueous humor is made behind the iris and must pass through the pupil to reach the drainage angle. In an eye with a shallow anterior chamber, mid-dilation in dim light increases contact between the iris and the lens. Aqueous is trapped behind the iris, which bows forward and seals the angle. Pressure rises fast, causing pain, corneal edema (halos), a fixed mid-dilated pupil from iris ischemia, and nausea. Open-angle glaucoma is different: the angle is open, outflow resistance rises slowly in the meshwork, and peripheral vision is lost without pain. Both damage the optic nerve and enlarge the cup.
whyNot: Correct.
Aqueous production is normal in glaucoma. The problem is blocked outflow.
Gradually rising outflow resistance in an open angle is primary open-angle glaucoma, which is painless and develops over years.
Red cells clogging the meshwork occur after hyphema from trauma. She has no injury or blood in the anterior chamber.

questions.stem: In her left eye, aqueous humor continues to be secreted while its drainage is blocked. Which of the following correctly pairs the site where aqueous humor is secreted with the channel through which it normally drains toward the veins?
options: Corneal endothelium, then the vortex veins
Iris pigment epithelium, then the central retinal vein
Lens epithelium, then the canal of Schlemm
Ciliary epithelium, then the canal of Schlemm
approach: Trace aqueous from start to finish: production, flow, drainage.
The nonpigmented ciliary epithelium secretes aqueous into the posterior chamber; it flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber.
It drains at the angle through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm and then to episcleral veins.
questions.why: The ciliary processes are covered by a two-layer epithelium, and the inner nonpigmented layer secretes aqueous humor into the posterior chamber. Aqueous passes through the pupil, nourishes the lens and cornea, and leaves mainly through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm, which empties into episcleral veins. A smaller amount leaves through the uveoscleral route. Tears are a separate system: the lacrimal gland, driven by CN VII parasympathetic fibers, makes the watery layer, and meibomian glands add the oily layer.
whyNot: The corneal endothelium pumps fluid out of the cornea to keep it clear; it does not make aqueous. Vortex veins drain the choroid.
The iris does not secrete aqueous, and the central retinal vein drains the inner retina, not the anterior chamber.
The lens epithelium maintains the lens and does not secrete aqueous, although the canal of Schlemm is correct for drainage.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her lifelong refractive error increased her risk for this condition. Which of the following best describes her refractive error?
options: Long eyeball with images focused in front of the retina
Short eyeball with images focused behind the retina
Unequal corneal curvature in different meridians
Stiffened lens with reduced ability to accommodate
approach: Farsightedness since childhood is hyperopia.
In hyperopia the eye is too short for its focusing power, so parallel light focuses behind the retina; convex lenses correct it.
A short eye has a crowded front segment and a shallow anterior chamber, which predisposes to angle closure.
questions.why: In hyperopia, the eye is short relative to the power of the cornea and lens, so light focuses behind the retina. Young people can overcome mild hyperopia by accommodating, but distance and near vision blur as accommodation fades. A short eye also has a shallow anterior chamber and a narrow angle, and the lens thickens with age, which makes angle closure more likely. Myopia is the opposite (eye too long, corrected with concave lenses). Astigmatism comes from uneven corneal curvature. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of lens elasticity that makes near work hard after about age 40.
whyNot: This is myopia, which is corrected with concave lenses. A long eye has a deep anterior chamber and is a risk factor for retinal detachment, not angle closure.
Correct.
This is astigmatism, which blurs vision at all distances and does not narrow the angle.
This is presbyopia, an age-related change that affects everyone over about 40 and is not a lifelong refractive error.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden, painless, complete loss of vision in his right eye that began 5 hours ago and has not improved. Intraocular pressure is 15 mm Hg in both eyes (normal 10 to 21). Which of the following is most likely on funduscopic examination of the right eye?
options: Scattered retinal hemorrhages with dilated tortuous veins
Deep optic disc cupping with a thin neuroretinal rim
Whitened retina with a red spot at the fovea
Normal retina with a bright plaque in an arteriole
approach: Sudden painless persistent monocular loss with an embolic source suggests central retinal artery occlusion.
Without blood flow, the inner retina becomes swollen and opaque white.
The fovea has no inner retinal layers, so the normal choroid shows through as a cherry-red spot.
questions.why: The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina. When an embolus, for example from atrial fibrillation or carotid plaque, blocks it, the inner retina becomes ischemic and swollen and looks pale or white. The fovea is thin and receives its blood from the choroid, so it stands out as a cherry-red spot. Amaurosis fugax is the transient version, often from carotid emboli, with vision returning within minutes. Central retinal vein occlusion causes painless vision loss with widespread retinal hemorrhages, swollen tortuous veins, and disc swelling.
whyNot: Widespread hemorrhages with swollen tortuous veins describe central retinal vein occlusion, which is linked to hypertension and diabetes rather than emboli.
Disc cupping develops slowly in glaucoma and causes gradual peripheral loss. His pressure is normal and the loss was sudden.
Correct.
A refractile cholesterol plaque in an arteriole with vision returning fits amaurosis fugax. His vision loss has persisted.

case: A 79-year-old woman comes to the physician because of distorted vision in her left eye for 10 days. Straight door frames look wavy, and there is a dark smudge in the center of what she sees. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. Two years ago she was told that she had yellow deposits under the retina in both eyes. Visual acuity is 20/200 in the left eye and 20/40 in the right. Peripheral vision is intact. Funduscopic examination of the left eye shows subretinal fluid and hemorrhage at the macula; both eyes show drusen. Fluorescein angiography shows a leaking choroidal neovascular membrane beneath the left macula. Diagnosis: neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration.

questions.stem: Which of the following most directly explains the rapid loss of central vision in her left eye?
options: Gradual atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
Opacification of the lens nucleus by protein aggregation
Tractional separation of the neurosensory retina
VEGF-driven choroidal vessel growth under the macula
approach: Drusen in both eyes mean she has had dry macular degeneration.
Sudden distortion (metamorphopsia) and central loss with fluid and blood under the macula mean the disease has turned wet.
Wet disease is driven by VEGF, which makes fragile new choroidal vessels grow through Bruch membrane and leak.
questions.why: Age-related macular degeneration damages the macula and spares peripheral vision. In the dry form, drusen (deposits between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane) and gradual atrophy cause slow central loss. In the wet form, ischemia and damage of the outer retina raise vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which drives new vessels from the choroid through Bruch membrane. These vessels leak fluid and bleed under the retina, so central vision distorts and falls quickly. Age and smoking are the main risk factors.
whyNot: Slow atrophy of the pigment epithelium is dry macular degeneration, which causes gradual loss over years, not in days.
Lens opacity is a cataract, which causes painless glare and blurred vision without metamorphopsia or subretinal blood.
Separation of the retina causes flashes, floaters, and a peripheral curtain of vision loss, not leaking vessels at the macula.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her remaining photoreceptors still respond to light. When a photon is absorbed by 11-cis retinal in a photoreceptor, which of the following sequences of events follows?
options: Decreased cGMP, closed sodium channels, hyperpolarization
Increased cGMP, opened sodium channels, depolarization
Increased cAMP, opened calcium channels, depolarization
Decreased cAMP, closed potassium channels, depolarization
approach: In the dark, high cGMP keeps sodium channels open (the dark current), so photoreceptors are depolarized and release glutamate.
Light converts 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal, activating opsin, which activates transducin and then phosphodiesterase.
Phosphodiesterase breaks down cGMP, the channels close, and the cell hyperpolarizes, releasing less glutamate.
questions.why: Photoreceptors work in reverse compared with most sensory receptors: light hyperpolarizes them. Light isomerizes 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal in rhodopsin (rods) or cone opsins. The activated opsin turns on the G protein transducin, which activates cGMP phosphodiesterase. cGMP falls, cGMP-gated sodium channels close, and the cell hyperpolarizes, cutting glutamate release onto bipolar cells. Retinal is made from vitamin A, so vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness first, because rods depend most on rhodopsin regeneration.
whyNot: Correct.
This describes the photoreceptor in the dark. Light lowers cGMP and closes the channels.
Phototransduction uses cGMP, not cAMP, and light hyperpolarizes photoreceptors rather than depolarizing them.
cAMP is not the second messenger here, and light causes hyperpolarization, not depolarization.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with high myopia has a sudden shower of new floaters and flashes of light in his right eye, followed by a dark curtain spreading across the upper part of his vision. Which of the following best explains his vision loss?
options: New choroidal vessels leaking beneath the macula
Inherited degeneration of rods beginning in the peripheral retina
Sensory retina separated from the pigment epithelium
Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery
approach: Flashes and floaters followed by a curtain of vision loss is the classic history of retinal detachment.
The neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium are attached only loosely, a remnant of the embryonic optic cup space.
A retinal tear lets fluid enter between these layers and lift the sensory retina away from its blood supply.
questions.why: The neural retina develops from the inner layer of the optic cup and the pigment epithelium from the outer layer, and the space between them never fully seals. In a rhegmatogenous detachment, the vitreous pulls on the retina and tears it (flashes from traction, floaters from blood or pigment). Fluid then enters through the tear and separates the sensory retina from the pigment epithelium and choroid, which feed the photoreceptors. High myopia is a key risk because the long eye has a thin, stretched retina. Retinitis pigmentosa is different: an inherited degeneration with night blindness and peripheral loss over years.
whyNot: Choroidal neovascularization is wet macular degeneration. It distorts central vision without flashes or a curtain.
Inherited rod degeneration is retinitis pigmentosa, which causes night blindness and tunnel vision over years with bone spicule pigment.
Correct.
Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless loss without flashes or floaters and shows a cherry-red spot.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has 1 day of pain, redness, and light sensitivity in his left eye. For 2 years he has had low back stiffness that is worst in the morning and improves with exercise. Slit-lamp examination shows inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber. Which of the following is most likely present in this patient?
options: HLA-DR3
HLA-B27
HLA-DR4
HLA-DQ2
approach: Inflammatory back pain in a young man suggests ankylosing spondylitis, a seronegative spondyloarthropathy.
Painful red eye with cells in the anterior chamber is anterior uveitis.
Both are tied to the MHC class I allele HLA-B27.
questions.why: Anterior uveitis (iritis) is inflammation of the iris and ciliary body, causing pain, redness around the cornea, photophobia, and cells in the anterior chamber. It is the most common extra-articular feature of the HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, such as ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis. Sarcoidosis and juvenile idiopathic arthritis also cause anterior uveitis. Posterior uveitis and chorioretinitis are more often infectious, such as toxoplasmosis and CMV retinitis in AIDS.
whyNot: HLA-DR3 is linked to type 1 diabetes, Graves disease, and lupus, not spondyloarthropathy.
Correct.
HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes. Rheumatoid arthritis spares the sacroiliac joints and lower spine.
HLA-DQ2 is linked to celiac disease.

dx: Temporal lobe brain abscess complicating chronic otitis media and mastoiditis
case: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of worsening headache for 10 days and trouble finding words for 2 days. He has had recurrent drainage from his left ear since childhood. His temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows foul-smelling pus in the left ear canal, a perforated left tympanic membrane, and tenderness over the left mastoid. He has word-finding difficulty and a right upper quadrant visual field defect in both eyes. Contrast MRI of the brain shows a 3-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe with surrounding edema. Aspirated pus grows streptococci and anaerobes. Diagnosis: temporal lobe brain abscess complicating chronic otitis media and mastoiditis.

questions.stem: By which of the following routes did the infection most likely reach his brain?
options: Bacteremic seeding through a right-to-left shunt
Extension through the posterior wall of the frontal sinus
Extension through the bony roof of the middle ear
Extension along olfactory nerves through the cribriform plate
approach: A single abscess next to a chronically infected ear and mastoid points to spread from a contiguous focus.
The roof of the middle ear and mastoid (tegmen tympani) is a thin plate of the temporal bone that lies directly under the temporal lobe.
Infection crosses this bone or travels in small veins to reach the temporal lobe; ear infections can also reach the cerebellum.
questions.why: Brain abscesses come from contiguous spread or blood-borne seeding. Contiguous spread is usually from the ear, mastoid, sinuses, or teeth, and it gives one abscess near the source: ear and mastoid infections cause temporal lobe or cerebellar abscesses, and frontal sinusitis or dental infections cause frontal lobe abscesses. Hematogenous spread, from endocarditis, lung infection, or a right-to-left shunt that bypasses the lung filter, often causes multiple abscesses. Typical organisms are streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes. Imaging shows a ring-enhancing lesion with edema.
whyNot: Right-to-left shunts allow bacteria to skip the lung filter and seed the brain, usually producing multiple abscesses. His source is next to the abscess.
Frontal sinus infection spreads to the frontal lobe, not the temporal lobe.
Correct.
The cribriform plate links the nasal cavity to the frontal lobe and olfactory bulbs, far from the temporal lobe.

questions.stem: His ear problems began at age 2 years with fever, ear pain, and a red, bulging tympanic membrane. Which of the following organisms most likely caused that first episode?
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Escherichia coli
approach: A bulging red tympanic membrane with fever in a toddler is acute otitis media.
Children are prone to it because their eustachian tubes are short, narrow, and more horizontal, so the middle ear does not drain well after a cold.
The usual organisms come from the nasopharynx: Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis.
questions.why: Acute otitis media follows eustachian tube dysfunction, usually after a viral upper respiratory infection. Fluid trapped in the middle ear becomes infected by bacteria that colonize the nasopharynx, most often Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Fluid that remains without signs of infection is otitis media with effusion and causes conductive hearing loss. Complications include perforation, mastoiditis, cholesteatoma, and spread into the skull, as in this patient.
whyNot: Correct.
Pseudomonas often grows from a chronically draining ear and causes otitis externa, but it is not a usual cause of a first acute middle ear infection.
Staphylococcus epidermidis is a skin commensal that infects implanted devices. It is not a middle ear pathogen in a healthy child.
Escherichia coli causes neonatal meningitis and urinary infections, not acute otitis media in toddlers.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus has had severe right ear pain and drainage for 6 weeks. His hemoglobin A1c is 10.4% (normal below 5.7%). Examination shows granulation tissue on the floor of the external ear canal and weakness of the entire right side of the face. CT shows erosion of the skull base. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Haemophilus influenzae
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
approach: An older diabetic patient with a painful draining ear canal, granulation tissue, and a cranial nerve palsy has malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa.
Infection spreads from the ear canal into the temporal bone and skull base, causing osteomyelitis that can damage CN VII and lower cranial nerves.
The classic organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
questions.why: Ordinary otitis externa (swimmer's ear) is infection of the ear canal skin, usually by Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus aureus, with pain when the tragus is pressed. In older patients with diabetes or immune compromise, Pseudomonas can invade through the canal floor into the temporal bone and skull base. This is malignant otitis externa, a skull base osteomyelitis that often causes facial nerve palsy first. Auricular perichondritis is a different Pseudomonas infection of the ear cartilage, often after a piercing through the upper ear.
whyNot: S. aureus is a common cause of simple otitis externa, but skull base osteomyelitis in an older diabetic patient is classically Pseudomonas.
S. pneumoniae causes acute otitis media and meningitis, not invasive infection starting in the ear canal.
Nontypeable H. influenzae causes acute otitis media in children, not necrotizing otitis externa.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman who has smoked for 40 years has 3 weeks of headache and new left arm weakness. She has no fever. Contrast MRI of the brain shows four round, ring-enhancing lesions of different sizes, each at the junction of the gray and white matter, with surrounding edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Meningioma
Metastatic carcinoma
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype
Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
approach: Several round lesions at the gray-white junction suggest blood-borne spread.
At the gray-white junction, arterioles narrow abruptly, so tumor emboli lodge there.
In adults, metastases are the most common intracranial tumors, and lung cancer is the most common source, which fits her smoking history.
questions.why: Brain metastases outnumber primary brain tumors in adults. Lung cancer, breast cancer, melanoma, kidney cancer, and colorectal cancer are the usual sources. Tumor cells arrive in arterial blood and lodge where vessels narrow at the gray-white junction, so metastases are often multiple, well circumscribed, and surrounded by edema. Ring enhancement can make them look like abscesses, but she has no fever and no infected source. Primary CNS lymphoma is a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, often linked to EBV in AIDS, and usually involves deep periventricular regions.
whyNot: Meningioma is an extra-axial, dural-based tumor that enhances uniformly. It does not form multiple ring lesions in the brain tissue.
Correct.
Glioblastoma is usually a single ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis that can cross the corpus callosum, not several separate lesions at the gray-white junction.
Primary CNS lymphoma tends to involve deep periventricular areas and is most often ring-enhancing in patients with AIDS.
